Prerogative

prih-ROG-uh-tiv -- stress on ROG; note the first syllable sounds like 'prih,' not 'pree'. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Prerogative is a right or privilege belonging exclusively to a particular person, office, or class.

Granting pardons is the governor's prerogative, a power the state constitution gives to no one else.

Worked Example

Under the orchestra's bylaws, only the conductor may choose the season's final program; the musicians may suggest pieces, but the last word belongs to her office alone.

That exclusive right, attached to a particular office, is a prerogative. Choosing the program is the conductor's prerogative -- a privilege that belongs to her role and to no one else's.

How Prerogative Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

privilege

privilege: a special right granted to a person or group

entitlement

entitlement: a guaranteed claim or right to something

authority

authority: the power or right to give orders and make decisions

Antonyms

obligation

obligation: something one is required to do

duty

duty: a task or responsibility one is bound to perform

How Strong Is It? — privilege → prerogative → entitlement

privilege vs. prerogative

privilege vs. prerogative: Privilege is broader and often weaker than prerogative -- privileges can be handed out widely and taken away, while a prerogative is an exclusive right built into a particular office or position.

entitlement vs. prerogative

entitlement vs. prerogative: Entitlement can sound even more absolute than prerogative: a prerogative is an exclusive right that comes with a role, while an entitlement is a guaranteed claim its holder can demand outright, no questions asked.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin prae-)

root — rog-

root — rog-: to ask, to propose (Latin rogare)

suffix — -ative

suffix — -ative: relating to (Latin -ativus)

Put it together

Put it together: Prerogative comes from Latin praerogativa -- literally 'asked before.' In ancient Rome, the praerogativa was the group of voters asked for its opinion first, before everyone else. From that head start grew the modern meaning: a special right that belongs to one office or class ahead of all others.

Root Check

Word Choice

Prerogative names a right that belongs exclusively to a particular role, office, or class: the crown's prerogative, a parent's prerogative, the editor's prerogative. In casual speech it gets watered down to mean any personal choice -- in formal writing and on the ISEE, keep it tied to a right that comes with a position.
